syllabus.quote: Describe state the points of a topic/give characteristics and main features

one_line: Say what it is, what it does or how it happens. Give enough separate, accurate points to match the marks. Give reasons only if the question asks for them.

points.text: In most Describe mark schemes, each correct point earns one mark. So a 4-mark Describe question needs about four separate points. One long sentence that says one thing is not enough.

cites.quote: As a description is generally a one-mark answer, candidates had to give three separate descriptions for full marks to be awarded.
Typically, one would expect a four mark question to require four individual points to be made.
Question 1 has four marks available for describing the structure of a cellular network so at least four points need to be made in the answer for full marks

points.text: Some mark schemes give one mark for a point, shown as (1st). They give a second mark for more detail about that same point, shown as (1). On those questions, four short points can often get 4 marks. Two points with more detail can also get 4 marks. 83 of the 387 Describe mark schemes from 2022 on use (1st) somewhere. None before 2022 use it.

cites.quote: A wind sensor/anemometer (1st) – is used to measure the direction of the wind (1)
It is interrogated by the inference engine (1st) – Using relevant rules//rules that apply (1)
Therefore, they could describe four individual functions or two in some depth, or three with a mixture of techniques.
This meant that candidates could gain full credit by either giving four descriptions or expanding on fewer descriptions.

points.text: Naming things is not describing them. Examiner reports say that answers which only name components do not get the higher marks. At least one mark scheme limits answers that only give names. It allows a maximum of 3 of 5 marks for naming events without descriptions. Say what each one is or does.

cites.quote: Max three for naming valid events without descriptions
Many responses indicated that candidates knew the names of the components but were unable to describe them in the detail required to gain the higher marks.
candidates were unable to describe the component, without relying on simply restating the component’s name.

points.text: Describe is about what and how. Explain adds why. You do not need a reason in a Describe answer unless the question asks for one, for example 'Describe, with reasons'. If it does, you cannot get full marks without the reasons.

cites.quote: Explain set out purposes or reasons/make the relationships between things clear/say why and/or how and support with relevant evidence
Candidates were asked to explain the differences rather than describe, so they were expected to give reasons for why the differences exist.
Describe, with reasons, the steps the manager takes when setting up this process.
Must have at least TWO reasons to obtain full marks
For each part, candidates had to describe the process and give a reason for its use for full marks to be awarded.

points.text: Examiner reports often say that students mix up Describe and Explain. The opposite mistake also loses marks. If the question asks why, a description of the thing itself gets few or no marks.

cites.quote: Many candidates failed to differentiate between, for example, questions where they were asked to describe and questions where they were asked to explain.
where a question asks why a protocol or process would be used, there is usually little or no credit given for describing the protocol or process itself since this does not answer the question ‘why?’.

points.text: Check what the question asks you to describe. For 'Describe how X is set up' or 'the process of', give the steps in order. For 'Describe the features' or 'the functions', say what X is or does. For 'Describe the benefits', give benefits, not uses. An answer about the wrong one gets no marks, even if it is true.

cites.quote: Good answers detailed the steps that would be taken to set up an electronic wallet. No details of the use of the wallet were required to gain marks.
some only identified methods of collecting the data without saying how they would be used for example, what data would be collected or who it would be collected from.
Common mistakes included descriptions of uses, inaccurate references to network performance and to illegal activities.
some focused on the use of the internet and remote learning, neither of which are features of a MOOC.

points.text: Do not repeat the question. Answers such as 'White box testing is used to test the code' or 'a sound sensor measures sound' get no mark. Add a detail that the question does not already give you.

cites.quote: Further, many candidates repeated the question, writing that ‘white box testing is used to test the code’. In general, statements that repeat the question are not given credit.
Candidates should avoid simply repeating the question in their response without further expansion; for example, a humidity sensor measures humidity and a sound sensor measures sound.

points.text: Vague words such as 'cheaper', 'more expensive' or 'work out the costs' do not get marks on their own. Say exactly what is cheaper, or name the exact cost. Use the correct technical term, not slang.

cites.quote: Some weaker responses contained responses such as ‘more expensive’ which is not enough at this level and statements such as this should always be expanded.
However, where candidates stated that a specific, named, cost could be avoided, this was awarded.
A common mistake was to give vague answers such as ‘work out the costs’.
candidates did not always focus as keenly as was required and gave vague answers that did not warrant any marks.
The use of what may be considered slang often renders answers meaningless.

points.text: Use the scenario. The question can be about a nuclear power plant, a bank's new customers or a table of data. Your points should fit that situation. A point that is true in general but wrong for the scenario loses the mark. A prepared answer that ignores the question gets only low marks.

cites.quote: The full range of marks is only available to candidates for answers referring to the scenario in the questions.
context also provides a restriction, as certain answers may be acceptable for one scenario, but not for another.
Many responses suggested a form of lookup validation. This would not be acceptable, as the account numbers are for new customers and so would not exist.
those who provided an answer they had prepared for, rather than for the question on the paper, were limited to low band marks.

points.text: Write descriptions as full sentences, with one point in each sentence. The Paper 3 reports say that you cannot give a description in short bullets. On one Paper 1 question, the examiners accepted a list of steps for a 'describe the process' question. But full sentences are the safe choice on both papers.

cites.quote: Descriptions or explanations can only be conveyed in full sentences.
Candidates should also be encouraged to write full sentences and discouraged from writing bulleted, short statements in their responses.
In the first, candidates listed (sometimes by creating a bulleted list) steps that would be taken, whilst others described the steps that had been taken. Either method was acceptable

points.text: If the question asks for a set number of things, for example 'Describe two reasons', the examiner marks only the first that many answers. Extra answers do not help. If you join two ideas with 'and', the second idea can count as a separate answer. So give each point its own sentence.

cites.quote: Typically, where candidates join two concepts together using ‘and’, the concept after the word ‘and’ is treated as a second answer, unless the piece after the ‘and’ is clearly an explanation or clarification of the piece before the ‘and’.
The question clearly stated that two reasons should be described so it was not possible to score full marks without giving two descriptions.
If, for example, the question asks for two reasons why an action may be taken, only the first two answers given by the candidate may be awarded marks.

question.quote: (b) Describe how a knowledge base is used in an expert system.

examples.context: Part (a) asked what is meant by the term knowledge base.

strong.sentence: The knowledge base holds the facts about the subject area of the expert system.

earns.quote: 4(b) Four from: • Knowledge base holds facts (1)

strong.sentence: These facts have been gathered from a human expert in that subject.

earns.quote: Knowledge base holds facts (1) gathered from an expert (1)

strong.sentence: When a user enters a query, the inference engine interrogates the knowledge base.

earns.quote: It is interrogated by the inference engine (1st)

strong.sentence: The inference engine only uses the rules that apply to that query.

earns.quote: It is interrogated by the inference engine (1st) – Using relevant rules//rules that apply (1)

weak.answer: The knowledge base stores information and rules. The expert system uses it to make decisions.
weak.why: 'Stores rules' matches a mark scheme point. 'Stores information' may get the 'holds facts' mark. The answer does not say that the facts come from an expert. It does not say that the inference engine interrogates the knowledge base. It also does not say that the inference engine uses only the relevant rules.

basis.quote: For example, whilst many candidates stated that the knowledge base holds facts, very few stated that these were sourced from experts. Similarly, candidates were aware that rules are used to interrogate the knowledge base, but very few stated that only the relevant rules were used.

examples.note: This is a 'describe how' question, so the marks are for what happens, not why. Two of the four marks are for more detail about an earlier point. These are 'gathered from an expert' and 'only relevant rules'. So precise detail earns as much as new points.

question.quote: The directors of a company wish to create a database of customers. They are not sure whether they should ask a computer programmer to produce custom written software or they should purchase off-the-shelf software. (a) Describe the features of custom written software.

strong.sentence: A programmer develops custom written software specially for one specific company, here the directors' company.

earns.quote: Software that is specially developed for a specific company/business

strong.sentence: The programmer makes it to fit that company's particular preferences and needs, such as the exact customer details the directors want to store.

earns.quote: It is made to accommodate that customer's particular preferences and needs

strong.sentence: The company gets support directly from the programmers who created it.

earns.quote: Support is obtained directly from the creators

strong.sentence: The company that commissions the software has to pay the development costs.

earns.quote: Development costs have to be paid for by client for whom its written/ commissioning company/business

weak.answer: Custom written software is more expensive. It is better than off-the-shelf software.
weak.why: 'More expensive' is a vague comparison with no detail. 'Better' is an opinion, not a feature. The cost point earns a mark only when it says who pays the development costs.

basis.quote: Some weaker responses contained responses such as ‘more expensive’ which is not enough at this level and statements such as this should always be expanded.

examples.note: A 'describe the features' question wants four separate facts about what the thing is. You do not need reasons. But each fact must be specific enough to match a mark scheme point.

thin_evidence: There is plenty of evidence. Describe is one of the most common command words on Papers 1 and 3. The mark schemes do not define the (1st) label. This guide reads it as a first point that a later linked point expands. That reading comes from how the mark schemes lay out the points. It also comes from examiner report comments about expanding fewer points.
